title: Inlet proxy: congestion synthesis & GPU backpressure sketch
body:
Context and motivation:

This is a loosely structured sketch for an "inlet proxy" — a thin front-line service that merges multi-region routing policy, capacity-aware admission, and short-term workload smoothing before handing requests to the serving mesh. Goal: keep end-to-end tail latency predictable while maximizing GPU utilization across regions and supporting graceful cross-region fallbacks.

Why a proxy?
- Centralizes early decisions (route, shard, admit vs queue) where we have fastest access to request metadata and routing policy state.
- Allows cheap, adaptive shaping (local shedding, short queueing, burst buffers) before expensive cluster-wide decisions.
- Avoids touching long-tailed scheduling decisions inside the GPU pools except when necessary.

Design goals (non-exhaustive):
- Safety-first: never push a GPU node beyond an empirically validated utilization envelope that increases token-drop/loss of KV cache effectiveness.
- Latency SLOs: prioritize short requests and interactive paths; allow throughput-oriented jobs to be queued/batched with capacity signals.
- Predictable multi-region fallbacks: if local region capacity drops, trigger a buffered, rate-limited spillover to secondary regions with prioritized lanes.
- Low-cost telemetry: rely on a few high-signal metrics rather than full per-request tracing in the hot path.

Primary signals we plan to use (ranked by preference):
- GPU occupancy (per-pool 1m / 15s aggregates): instantaneous utilization + recent derivative.
- Local queue depth (proxy-level per-priority queue counts + per-model small-window ingress rates).
- Estimated tail token cost (amortized per-model token-per-step distribution; used for cost-aware shedding).
- KV cache hit rate on the serving side (proxy keeps a moving estimate via periodic poll).
- Recent observed tails (p95/p99 server processing latency reported by SRE heartbeats).
- Request metadata (model, max_tokens, streaming vs batch, customer tier).

Admission primitives considered:
- Elastic tokenbank (per-customer and per-route): tokens refill at a rate derived from committed capacity and dynamic pool headroom. Unlike a classic fixed tokenbucket, this one has a refill rate that can be nudged by GPU signals.
- Short-term queuing with hedged pop: small in-proxy queues (ms->few-seconds) with hedging slots for latency-critical requests.
- Soft admit bands: configurable thresholds (green/yellow/red) that map to progressive mitigation (no action, slow-path queues, drop-or-defer).
- Burst windows: allow one-off bursts above steady-state for short-lived spikes, tracked via a sliding credit ledger (decays fast).

Admission algorithm (sketch):
1) Enrich request: tag with model profile, expected avg_token_cost, priority band (from auth/pricing).
2) Check local tokenbank for customer/route: if tokens available, tentatively admit (reserve token cost).
3) Re-check aggregated GPU headroom for target pool: if headroom negative or derivative rising fast, route to slow-path queue or attempt spillover.
4) If slow-path queue length > threshold for that band, apply cost-aware shedding: 1) attempt to route to alternate compatible model (quantized), 2) fallback to remote region (rate-limited), 3) finally reject with graceful error suggesting retry/backoff or lower-cost model.
5) Upon admission success, decrement reserved bank, issue lightweight admission token to downstream runtime (idempotent).

Control loop and tuning knobs:
- Control loop frequency: mix of fast local gating (100ms–1s) and a stabilization window (30s–2m) for refill adjustments. Fast loop uses instantaneous occupancy+queue slope; slow loop smooths refill rates to avoid oscillations.
- Band thresholds: start conservative. Example: green < 70% occupancy, yellow 70–85%, red > 85% or slope > 5%/15s.
- Refill policy: baseline refill derived from committed capacity; if GPU pool underutilized for 60s, bump refill by small % to drain queues; if overutilized, cut refill aggressively and propagate backpressure upstream.
- Hedging policy: latency-critical requests get 1 extra hedged attempt to other pools when queue depth crosses a p90 threshold.

Instrumentation and telemetry (practical):
- Minimal hot-path metrics (exposed per-proxy): in-flight count by band, short-queue length, reserve-errors, spillover-rate.
- Periodic (10s–30s): pool-level occupancy, KV cache hit rate, tail-latency markers.
- Alerts derived from combined signals rather than single metric thresholds (e.g., occupancy>85% + queue growth > 20% over 30s).
- Traces: sample 1 in N requests for full trace; prefer histogram-based metrics for SLOs.

Prototype experiments to run (order):
- Local microbench: fake GPU backend that exposes occupancy profiles. Feed synthetic traces with mixed short/long requests and measure admitted vs dropped, p95, utilization. Vary refill aggressiveness and queue depth.
- Cheap spillover test: implement remote-region forwarder with rate-limiter and observe end-to-end latency and cost delta. 
- KV-aware shaping: simulate varying KV-hit rates and measure the point where cache degradation increases per-token latency by >10%.

Known trade-offs and unknowns:
- Risk of oscillation: naive refill changes can cause waves (we need hysteresis and derivative damping).
- Cross-region consistency: how often should proxies share state? Full global tokenbanks are expensive; prefer local leaders and probabilistic spillover.
- Fairness: balancing per-customer fairness vs global efficiency is a policy decision (reserved capacity vs best-effort).
- Accurate cost estimates: model token-cost distributions are fuzzy; wrong estimates could over-shed. Need a feedback path that corrects per-model cost estimates.

Open questions for sync with SRE/Serving teams:
- What exact occupancy telemetry can serving expose with <100ms freshness? (ask SRE)
- How to represent model compatibility sets for spillover without a huge N^2 matrix? (catalog heuristics/profiles?)
- SLA behavior: when a Dedicated customer has reserved capacity but local region is saturated, does policy permit forced local routing or always allow cross-region fallback?

Implementation notes / quick wins:
- Start as a sidecar routing layer in front of gateways (simpler rollout). Keep the admission state local; leader election only for aggregated sharding.
- Build tokenbank store as simple in-memory with optional Redis backing for cross-proxy sharing in later phases.
- Expose a /debug/live view showing current refill rates, band thresholds, and per-customer credits to aid on-call.

Action items (short):
- [Aisha] build microbench harness and fake-backend (2 weeks).
- [Marco] confirm GPU occupancy metrics and revisit frequency with SRE (this week).
- [Liam] prototype small in-proxy queueing and hedging codepath (spike, 1 week).
- [Sofia] draft policy doc for per-customer refill defaults and reserved vs shared capacity rules (1 week).

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Consider naming the green/yellow/red bands as laminar/eddy/stall to avoid policy-language friction.
- Small queues should be careful about memory blowups—cap by token-cost rather than request count when possible.
- Watch out for cases where quantized fallback increases per-request compute enough to negate the benefit (i.e., avoid swapping to tiny-quant models if token count still high).

References & threads:
- Slack: #platform-routing: "region spillover and hedging" (thread id 2834)
- Confluence: capacity-synthesis/notes
- Jira: JIRA-PLAT-4987 (proto ingress shaping)

This is intentionally an iteration-stage sketch; looking for quick feedback on the high-signal knobs (refill hysteresis, queue SLOs, and minimal telemetry set) before turning this into a full design doc.

-- Aisha
